little_women.summary: Christmas finds the four March sisters living in reduced circumstances with their mother while their father serves in the Civil War. The book traces the sisters from adolescence into adulthood through domestic episodes, friendships, illnesses, romances, work, and quarrels: Meg wants comfort and marriage, Jo pursues writing and independence, Beth centers herself on home and music, and Amy aims for artistic and social success. Their lives become closely tied to their wealthy neighbor Laurie Laurence, whose friendship with Jo develops into a rejected proposal and later a marriage to Amy after both mature through disappointment and travel. Major turning points include Mr. March’s illness, Beth’s scarlet fever and eventual death, Meg’s marriage to John Brooke, Jo’s literary ambitions in New York, and the gradual reshaping of the sisters’ childhood hopes into more practical adult lives. In the final chapters, Jo inherits Aunt March’s estate, marries Professor Bhaer, and turns Plumfield into a school, while the extended family settles into a stable network of marriages, children, and shared household life.

chapters.title: I. Playing Pilgrims.
chapters.summary: The four March sisters talk by the fire about Christmas and their family's poverty while their father serves in the war. Each girl complains about her work and wishes for small luxuries, but they decide to spend their Christmas money on gifts for their mother instead of themselves. The chapter introduces the sisters' personalities through their arguments, games, and home theatricals, then ends with Mrs. March returning home to the lively household.
moments: "We haven't got father, and shall not have him for a long time."

"I hate to think I've got to grow up, and be Miss March, and wear long gowns, and look as prim as a China-aster! It's bad enough to be a girl, anyway, when I like boys' games and work and manners! I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy; and it's worse than ever now, for I'm dying to go and fight with papa, and I can only stay at home and knit, like a poky old woman!"
"let's each get her something for Christmas, and not get anything for ourselves."

chapters.title: II. A Merry Christmas.
chapters.summary: The March sisters wake on Christmas morning to find small books from their mother under their pillows, and they promise to read from them each day. Mrs. March asks the girls to give their breakfast to a starving family nearby, and they carry food, firewood, and comfort to the Hummels before returning home to exchange simple gifts with their mother. The rest of the day is spent preparing for the sisters' Christmas play, with Jo taking the lead in the evening performance.
moments: "My girls, will you give them your breakfast as a Christmas present?"
"I'm so glad you came before we began!"
"That's loving our neighbor better than ourselves, and I like it," said Meg, as they set out their presents, while their mother was upstairs collecting clothes for the poor Hummels.

chapters.title: III. The Laurence Boy.
chapters.summary: Meg and Jo March prepare for a New Year's Eve dance with borrowed accessories, damaged gloves, and a failed attempt to curl Meg's hair. At the party, Meg joins the dancing while Jo hides in a curtained recess to keep the burn on her dress out of sight. There she meets Laurie Laurence, the boy who lives next door, and the two quickly become comfortable with each other as they talk about travel, school, names, and the party around them.
moments: "You must have gloves, or I won't go," cried Meg decidedly.
"I'm not Mr. Laurence, I'm only Laurie."
"I hate it! Nothing but grinding or skylarking. And I don't like the way fellows do either, in this country."

chapters.title: IV. Burdens.
chapters.summary: The March sisters struggle to return to work and routine after the holidays. Meg resents her poverty and job caring for spoiled children, while Jo tries to keep the family cheerful as she works for Aunt March and spends stolen hours reading in the old library. The chapter explains each sister’s burdens and desires: Meg longs for luxury, Jo wants freedom and achievement, Beth quietly cares for the household and dreams of music lessons, and Amy worries over her appearance and pursues drawing.
moments: "We can't give up our girls for a dozen fortunes. Rich or poor, we will keep together and be happy in one another."

"Jo's ambition was to do something very splendid; what it was she had no idea, as yet, but left it for time to tell her; and, meanwhile, found her greatest affliction in the fact that she couldn't read, run, and ride as much as she liked."
"I know I'll get my music some time, if I'm good."

chapters.title: V. Being Neighborly.
chapters.summary: Jo decides to visit the lonely Laurence boy after seeing him sick and isolated in the house next door. She brings food and Beth’s kittens, tidies Laurie’s room, and spends the afternoon talking with him about family, books, and life at home with the March sisters. Their visit begins a friendship between the two households and gives Laurie a sense of warmth and companionship he has been missing.
moments: "We'll never draw that curtain any more, and I give you leave to look as much as you like. I just wish, though, instead of peeping, you'd come over and see us.
"We are not strangers, we are neighbors, and you needn't think you'd be a bother. We want to know you, and I've been trying to do it this ever so long.
"A fellow can't live on books," said Laurie, shaking his head, as he perched on a table opposite.

chapters.title: VI. Beth finds the Palace Beautiful.
chapters.summary: The March girls and Laurie grow close, and the Laurence house becomes part of their daily lives. Beth is terrified of old Mr. Laurence, but he notices her love of music and invites her to practice on his piano when the house is empty. After Beth secretly makes him a pair of embroidered slippers to thank him, Mr. Laurence gives her the piano that belonged to his dead granddaughter, and Beth overcomes her fear enough to go to his study and embrace him.
moments: “O sir, they do care, very, very much!”
“I had a little girl once, with eyes like these. God bless you, my dear! Good day, madam;” and away he went, in a great hurry.

If you will believe me, she went and knocked at the study-door before she gave herself time to think; and when a gruff voice called out, “Come in!” she did go in, right up to Mr. Laurence, who looked quite taken aback, and held out her hand, saying, with only a small quaver in her voice, “I came to thank you, sir, for—” But she didn't finish; for he looked so friendly that she forgot her speech, and, only remembering that he had lost the little girl he loved, she put both arms round his neck, and kissed him.

chapters.title: VII. Amy's Valley of Humiliation.
chapters.summary: Amy borrows money from Meg to buy pickled limes, which have become a school fad and a form of social currency among the girls. At school, Jenny Snow reports her to Mr. Davis, who confiscates the limes, strikes Amy's hand in front of the class, and forces her to stand on the platform as punishment. Humiliated, Amy leaves the school and refuses to return, while Mrs. March comforts her but also warns her against vanity and disobedience.
moments: "Miss March, hold out your hand."
"For the first time in her life she had been struck; and the disgrace, in her eyes, was as deep as if he had knocked her down."
"You are getting to be rather conceited, my dear, and it is quite time you set about correcting it."

chapters.title: VIII. Jo Meets Apollyon.
chapters.summary: Jo and Meg go to the theatre with Laurie and refuse to take Amy, which leads Amy to burn the book of stories Jo has spent years writing. Jo refuses Amy’s apology and carries her anger into the next day, when Amy follows Jo and Laurie to the river to skate. Amy falls through thin ice, and Laurie and Jo rescue her, forcing Jo to confront the danger her resentment created.
moments: "You wicked, wicked girl! I never can write it again, and I'll never forgive you as long as I live."
"Bring a rail; quick, quick!"

chapters.title: IX. Meg goes to Vanity Fair.
chapters.summary: Meg prepares for a two-week visit with the wealthy Moffat family and worries about her plain clothes beside their fashionable things. At the party she feels ashamed of her old dress, but Laurie’s flowers and her mother’s note restore her spirits until she overhears the women gossiping about her poverty and speculating that Mrs. March hopes Meg will marry Laurie for his money. The visit changes how Meg sees wealth, class, and her friendship with Laurie, and leaves her torn between pride in her family and a growing desire for luxury.
moments: "Mrs M. has made her plans, I dare say, and will play her cards well, early as it is. The girl evidently doesn't think of it yet," said Mrs. Moffat.
"She's proud, but I don't believe she'd mind, for that dowdy tarlatan is all she has got. She may tear it to-night, and that will be a good excuse for offering a decent one."
"Those foolish, yet well-meant words, had opened a new world to Meg, and much disturbed the peace of the old one, in which, till now, she had lived as happily as a child."

chapters.title: X. The P. C. and P. O.
chapters.summary: The March sisters spend the spring gardening and inventing games and clubs at home. They hold a meeting of their secret society, the Pickwick Club, where they read pieces for their homemade newspaper, including poems, stories, mock reports, and jokes that tease one another and describe events in the household. At the end of the meeting, Jo proposes Theodore Laurence for honorary membership in the club, which starts a debate among the girls about letting a boy into their private world.
moments: "I propose Mr. Theodore Laurence as an honorary member of the P. C. Come now, do have him."

"Sir, I give you my word as a gentleman, Laurie won't do anything of the sort. He likes to write, and he'll give a tone to our contributions, and keep us from being sentimental, don't you see? We can do so little for him, and he does so much for us, I think the least we can do is to offer him a place here, and make him welcome if he comes."

"My lord, you scornfully bade me claim your daughter when I could boast as high a name and vast a fortune as the Count Antonio. I can do more; for even your ambitious soul cannot refuse the Earl of Devereux and De Vere, when he gives his ancient name and boundless wealth in return for the beloved hand of this fair lady, now my wife."

chapters.title: XI. Experiments.
chapters.summary: The March sisters begin a week-long experiment in doing no work during their summer vacation. Each girl spends her time idly and soon becomes restless, quarrelsome, and dissatisfied while Mrs. March quietly keeps the house running for them. By the end of the week, Mrs. March withdraws from household duties entirely, forcing the girls to cook, clean, and manage the home themselves, which quickly leads to mistakes, confusion, and Beth's grief after her neglected canary dies.
moments: "You may try your experiment for a week, and see how you like it. I think by Saturday night you will find that all play and no work is as bad as all work and no play."
"Mother isn't sick, only very tired, and she says she is going to stay quietly in her room all day, and let us do the best we can."
"It's all my fault—I forgot him—there isn't a seed or a drop left. O Pip! O Pip! how could I be so cruel to you?"

chapters.title: XII. Camp Laurence
chapters.summary: The March sisters receive letters and invitations that shape their day. Jo is deeply encouraged by a note from Marmee praising her efforts to control her temper, and Laurie invites the sisters to a riverside picnic with his English friends. At Camp Laurence, the group rows, plays croquet, and socializes, but Jo nearly loses her temper during an argument with Fred Vaughn after he cheats during the game.
moments:
"My dear:

"I write a little word to tell you with how much satisfaction I watch your efforts to control your temper. You say nothing about your trials, failures, or successes, and think, perhaps, that no one sees them but the Friend whose help you daily ask, if I may trust the well-worn cover of your guide-book. I, too, have seen them all, and heartily believe in the sincerity of your resolution, since it begins to bear fruit. Go on, dear, patiently and bravely, and always believe that no one sympathizes more tenderly with you than your loving

"Mother."
"That does me good! that's worth millions of money and pecks of praise. O Marmee, I do try! I will keep on trying, and not get tired, since I have you to help me."
"We don't cheat in America, but you can, if you choose," said Jo angrily.

chapters.title: XIII. Castles in the Air.
chapters.summary: Laurie follows the March sisters to a grove where they hold meetings of their "Busy Bee Society," bringing work and books to the hill they call the "Delectable Mountain." The group talks about the futures they imagine for themselves: Laurie wants a life in music, Meg dreams of wealth and comfort, Jo wants fame as a writer, Beth wants her family to stay together, and Amy plans to become a great artist. Laurie also admits that he hates the business career his grandfather has chosen for him and wants the freedom to make his own life.
moments: "Wouldn't it be fun if all the castles in the air which we make could come true, and we could live in them?" said Jo, after a little pause.

"I want to do something splendid before I go into my castle,—something heroic or wonderful, that won't be forgotten after I'm dead. I don't know what, but I'm on the watch for it, and mean to astonish you all, some day.
"He wants me to be an India merchant, as he was, and I'd rather be shot."

chapters.title: XIV. Secrets.
chapters.summary: Jo secretly takes two stories to a newspaper office and tells Laurie she hopes to be published. Laurie confides that he knows Meg's glove is in Mr. Brooke's pocket, which convinces Jo that Meg and Mr. Brooke may be falling in love, and she becomes upset at the thought of Meg leaving the family. Jo also warns Laurie about spending time with fashionable young men and billiard halls because she fears his money and strong will could lead him into trouble.
moments: "Well, I've left two stories with a newspaper man, and he's to give his answer next week," whispered Jo, in her confidant's ear.
Laurie bent, and whispered three words in Jo's ear, which produced a comical change.
"Because if you care much about riches, you will never go and marry a poor man," said Jo, frowning at Laurie, who was mutely warning her to mind what she said.

chapters.title: XV. A Telegram.
chapters.summary: A telegram arrives saying Mr. March is dangerously ill in a Washington hospital, and Mrs. March quickly prepares to leave for him. The household shifts from boredom to crisis as the girls, Laurie, and their neighbors organize money, supplies, and travel arrangements. Jo secretly cuts off and sells her hair to raise money for her father’s care, showing how far the family will go to support him.
moments: "Your husband is very ill. Come at once.
"I shall go at once, but it may be too late. O children, children, help me to bear it!"
"That's my contribution towards making father comfortable and bringing him home!"

chapters.title: XVI. Letters.
chapters.summary: Mrs. March leaves home to care for her sick husband in Washington, and the four sisters try to follow her instructions to stay busy, help one another, and manage the household without complaint. After an emotional farewell, the girls settle into new responsibilities and receive improving news about their father through Mr. Brooke’s daily bulletins. The chapter closes with a series of letters from Meg, Jo, Beth, Amy, and Hannah, each showing how the family is coping with the separation and how the sisters are changing under the pressure of the crisis.
moments: "Go on with your work as usual, for work is a blessed solace. Hope and keep busy; and whatever happens, remember that you never can be fatherless."
"I read my little book, felt better, resolved not to let the sun set on my anger, and ran over to tell Laurie I was sorry."

"Head, you may think, Heart, you may feel,

But, Hand, you shall work alway!'"

chapters.title: XVII. Little Faithful.
chapters.summary: Beth keeps the March household running while her sisters drift back into comfort after their first burst of discipline during their mother's absence. When the others put off visiting the poor Hummel family, Beth goes alone, witnesses the death of the Hummels' baby, and returns home showing signs of scarlet fever after caring for the sick children. The family calls Dr. Bangs, sends Amy to Aunt March's house to avoid infection, and Jo blames herself for neglecting the duties she promised to take on.
moments: "Oh, Jo, the baby's dead!"
"Scarlet fever, ma'am. Ought to have called me before," he said crossly.
"Jo, please;" and Beth leaned her head against her sister, with a contented look, which effectually settled that point.

chapters.title: XVIII. Dark Days.
chapters.summary: Beth falls dangerously ill with scarlet fever, and the March sisters struggle to care for her while keeping the truth from their mother, who is away with Mr. March. As Beth grows delirious and Dr. Bangs warns that Mrs. March should be sent for, Jo breaks down under the fear of losing her sister. Laurie secretly telegraphs Mrs. March to come home, bringing hope back into the house as the family waits through a long winter night for Beth’s condition to change.
moments: "If Mrs. March can leave her husband, she'd better be sent for."
"I've sent for mother," said Jo, tugging at her rubber boots with a tragical expression.
"I telegraphed to your mother yesterday, and Brooke answered she'd come at once, and she'll be here to-night, and everything will be all right. Aren't you glad I did it?"

chapters.title: XIX. Amy's Will.
chapters.summary: Amy lives with Aunt March while Beth is ill at home, and she struggles with the old woman's rigid routines, lonely house, and demanding pets. Esther, the French maid, befriends her, tells her that Aunt March plans to leave her valuables to the March girls, and helps Amy create a private place for prayer and reflection. Feeling separated from her family and newly determined to behave well, Amy decides to write her own will and asks Laurie to read it.
moments: "To you and your sisters. I know it; Madame confides in me; I witnessed her will, and it is to be so," whispered Esther, smiling.

"Do you think so? Oh, I'll be a lamb, if I can only have that lovely ring! It's ever so much prettier than Kitty Bryant's. I do like Aunt March, after all;" and Amy tried on the blue ring with a delighted face, and a firm resolve to earn it.
"I want you to read that, please, and tell me if it is legal and right. I felt that I ought to do it, for life is uncertain and I don't want any ill-feeling over my tomb."

chapters.title: XX. Confidential.
chapters.summary: Mrs. March returns home to find Beth recovering, and the family settles into relief after days of fear and exhaustion. At Aunt March's house, Amy talks with her mother about trying to overcome her selfishness, using the turquoise ring Aunt March gave her as a reminder of her resolution. Later, Jo tells Mrs. March that Mr. Brooke loves Meg, and Mrs. March admits that he has already spoken to the family, though she insists Meg is too young to become engaged and should wait before making any commitment.
moments: "He is a truly excellent young man, and we could not refuse to listen to him; but I will not consent to Meg's engaging herself so young."
"I've thought a great deal lately about my 'bundle of naughties,' and being selfish is the largest one in it; so I'm going to try hard to cure it, if I can."
"Your father and I have agreed that she shall not bind herself in any way, nor be married, before twenty."

chapters.title: XXI. Laurie makes Mischief, and Jo makes Peace.
chapters.summary: Jo struggles to keep Meg's secret about Mr. Brooke while Laurie teases her until he discovers it concerns Meg and Brooke. Laurie retaliates by forging love letters between Meg and Brooke, which humiliates Meg and forces Mrs. March to intervene, question Meg about her feelings, and make Laurie apologize. After the family settles the misunderstanding, Jo visits Laurie and finds him fighting with his grandfather over the prank and his refusal to explain himself.
moments: "It's all a mistake—he didn't send it. O Jo, how could you do it?"
"I don't believe Brooke ever saw either of these letters. Teddy wrote both, and keeps yours to crow over me with, because I wouldn't tell him my secret."
"I don't intend to stay here long, any way. I'll slip off and take a journey somewhere, and when grandpa misses me he'll come round fast enough."

chapters.title: XXII. Pleasant Meadows.
chapters.summary: Beth recovers enough strength to rejoin the family as Christmas approaches, and Jo and Laurie prepare elaborate surprises to celebrate her improvement. On Christmas Day, Mr. March unexpectedly returns home with Mr. Brooke, and the family gathers for a joyful dinner and evening by the fire. Mr. March speaks to each daughter about how she has changed during the past year, praising Meg’s work, Jo’s growing steadiness, Amy’s thoughtfulness, and Beth’s quiet spirit before Beth closes the evening by singing at the piano again.
moments: "I'm so full of happiness, that, if father was only here, I couldn't hold one drop more," said Beth, quite sighing with contentment as Jo carried her off to the study to rest after the excitement, and to refresh herself with some of the delicious grapes the "Jungfrau" had sent her.
But it was too late; the study door flew open, the little red wrapper appeared on the threshold,—joy put strength into the feeble limbs,—and Beth ran straight into her father's arms.

"I read in 'Pilgrim's Progress' to-day, how, after many troubles, Christian and Hopeful came to a pleasant green meadow, where lilies bloomed all the year round, and there they rested happily, as we do now, before they went on to their journey's end," answered Beth; adding, as she slipped out of her father's arms, and went slowly to the instrument, "It's singing time now, and I want to be in my old place. I'll try to sing the song of the shepherd-boy which the Pilgrims heard. I made the music for father, because he likes the verses."

chapters.title: XXIII. Aunt March settles the Question.
chapters.summary: Meg and Jo talk about John Brooke's interest in Meg, and Meg rehearses the refusal she plans to give him if he proposes. When Brooke arrives, he confesses his love, and Meg first wavers, then pushes him away after feeling annoyed by his confidence. Aunt March interrupts and warns Meg that she will lose any inheritance if she marries Brooke, but Meg openly defends him and declares that she will marry whom she chooses.
moments: "I won't trouble you, I only want to know if you care for me a little, Meg. I love you so much, dear," added Mr. Brooke tenderly.
"I shall marry whom I please, Aunt March, and you can leave your money to any one you like," she said, nodding her head with a resolute air.
"My John wouldn't marry for money, anymore than I would. We are willing to work, and we mean to wait."

chapters.title: XXIV. Gossip.
chapters.summary: Three years after the war, the March family has settled into a quieter life. Meg prepares to marry John Brooke and move into the small house he has furnished for them, while the family helps set up the home and discusses the practical work of marriage and housekeeping. Jo continues writing and caring for Beth, Amy studies art while living with Aunt March, and Laurie drifts through college life, still closely tied to the March sisters.
moments: "But somehow envy and discontent soon vanished when she thought of all the patient love and labor John had put into the little home awaiting her; and when they sat together in the twilight, talking over their small plans, the future always grew so beautiful and bright that she forgot Sallie's splendor, and felt herself the richest, happiest girl in Christendom."

"The girls gave their hearts into their mother's keeping, their souls into their father's; and to both parents, who lived and labored so faithfully for them, they gave a love that grew with their growth, and bound them tenderly together by the sweetest tie which blesses life and outlives death."
"'Mother and I have talked that over, and I have made up my mind to try her way first.'"

chapters.title: XXV. The First Wedding.
chapters.summary: Meg March marries John Brooke in a small home wedding surrounded by her family and close friends. The chapter follows the preparations, the ceremony, and the celebration, with attention to the changes in the sisters as they grow older and begin to leave childhood behind. During the reception, Meg persuades Laurie to promise that he will refuse wine when young women offer it, a pledge he keeps afterward, and the chapter ends with Meg leaving for her new home with John.
moments: "I don't want a fashionable wedding, but only those about me whom I love, and to them I wish to look and be my familiar self."
"I promise, Mrs. Brooke!"

chapters.title: XXVI. Artistic Attempts.
chapters.summary: Amy throws herself into one artistic pursuit after another, from pen-and-ink drawing and painting to sculpture and sketching from nature. Her failures and persistence teach her the difference between enthusiasm and real talent, while her desire to become an accomplished lady draws her toward wealthy society and fashionable manners. She plans an elaborate outing for her drawing classmates despite her family's doubts about the expense and effort, and the household struggles to prepare for the event.
moments: "If I can't have it as I like, I don't care to have it at all. I know that I can carry it out perfectly well, if you and the girls will help a little; and I don't see why I can't if I'm willing to pay for it," said Amy, with the decision which opposition was apt to change into obstinacy.
"You don't care to make people like you, to go into good society, and cultivate your manners and tastes. I do, and I mean to make the most of every chance that comes.

"Very well, Amy; if your heart is set upon it, and you see your way through without too great an outlay of money, time, and temper, I'll say no more. Talk it over with the girls, and whichever way you decide, I'll do my best to help you."

chapters.title: XXVII. Literary Lessons.
chapters.summary: Jo discovers that sensational stories can earn money after reading a popular newspaper tale at a lecture. She writes a melodramatic story, wins a hundred-dollar prize, and uses the money to send Beth and Mrs. March to the seaside. Encouraged by the success, Jo sells her novel to a publisher who demands heavy cuts, and she revises the manuscript according to conflicting advice from her family, reshaping the book in hopes of publication.
moments: "I think you and I could do as well as that if we tried," returned Jo, amused at his admiration of the trash.
For a minute she stared at it as if it had been a snake, then she read her letter and began to cry.
"Send Beth and mother to the seaside for a month or two," answered Jo promptly.

chapters.title: XXVIII. Domestic Experiences.
chapters.summary: Meg throws herself into running her new household and tries to become the perfect wife, but her efforts leave her exhausted and anxious about money, meals, and housekeeping. After spending a disastrous day trying to make currant jelly, she breaks down when John unexpectedly brings a guest home to dinner, and the couple quarrel over responsibility, hospitality, and pride. By the end of the chapter, both Meg and John privately decide the other has failed in marital duty, and they settle into a tense silence instead of apologizing.
moments: "The—the jelly won't jell and I don't know what to do!"
"A man to dinner, and everything in a mess! John Brooke, how could you do such a thing?"
"You must get yourself out of the scrape as you can; I'm too used up to 'exert' myself for any one."

chapters.title: XXIX. Calls.
chapters.summary: Amy drags Jo out to return social calls, coaching her on how to dress and behave among wealthier neighbors. Jo obeys at first by becoming stiff and silent at the Chesters', then swings the other way at the Lambs', joking freely about the family's money-saving habits and Amy's improvised clothes and riding adventures. Amy is mortified because Jo's honesty and mockery expose details she believes should stay private, widening the difference between their ideas about class, manners, and pride.
moments: "What a haughty, uninteresting creature that oldest Miss March is!" was the unfortunately audible remark of one of the ladies, as the door closed upon their guests.
"Oh, Amy painted it; you can't buy those soft shades, so we paint ours any color we like. It's a great comfort to have an artistic sister."

"You needn't go and tell them all our little shifts, and expose our poverty in that perfectly unnecessary way. You haven't a bit of proper pride, and never will learn when to hold your tongue and when to speak," said Amy despa

chapters.title: XXX. Consequences.
chapters.summary: Amy is given charge of the art table at Mrs. Chester's fair, but Mrs. Chester and May push her aside after hearing that the March girls mocked May. Amy moves to the flower table, struggles through the fair in humiliation, and decides to answer the insult with kindness by returning her artwork to May's table. Jo and Laurie rally support for Amy on the second night of the fair, turning her neglected corner into the busiest part of the room and restoring her spirits.
moments: "It shall be as you please, Mrs. Chester. I'll give up my place here at once, and attend to the flowers, if you like."
"Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself."

"You may have them, and welcome, without asking, if you want them. I was just thinking I'd offer to put them back, for they belong to your table rather than mine. Here they are; please take them, and forgive me if I was hasty in carrying them away last night."

chapters.title: XXXI. Our Foreign Correspondent.
chapters.summary: Amy writes home from London, Paris, and Germany during her trip abroad with Aunt March and Florence. She describes the voyage across the Atlantic, sightseeing in England and France, shopping, museums, parks, and social outings, and she reconnects with Laurie’s English friends Fred and Frank Vaughn, who begin accompanying the family through Europe. The letters show Amy enjoying wealth, travel, and society while trying to develop her taste in art and manners, and they introduce Fred Vaughn as an important companion during her travels.
moments: Who do you think came in, as we were at tea? Laurie's English friends, Fred and Frank Vaughn!
Well, we were hardly settled here, when he turned up again, saying he had come for a holiday, and was going to Switzerland.
Fred is very entertaining, and is altogether the most agreeable young man I ever knew,—except Laurie, whose manners are more charming.

chapters.title: XXXII. Tender Troubles.
chapters.summary: Mrs. March asks Jo to find out why Beth has become quiet and sorrowful. Jo watches Beth and convinces herself that Beth is secretly in love with Laurie after seeing her react to him with unusual emotion. While Laurie visits the family, Jo studies his behavior toward Beth and begins imagining a future match between them, even as she and Laurie fall into a long conversation about flirting, society girls, and their own friendship.
moments: "How strong and well and happy that dear boy looks."
"Mercy on me, Beth loves Laurie!" she said, sitting down in her own room, pale with the shock of the discovery which she believed she had just made.

"No, thank you, sir; you're very charming, but you've no more stability than a weathercock; so you needn't write touching notes, and smile in that insinuating way, for it won't do a bit of good, and I won't have it."

chapters.title: XXXIII. Jo's Journal.
chapters.summary: Jo arrives in New York to work as a governess in Mrs. Kirke's boarding house. She settles into her small attic room, struggles through her first days teaching the children, and begins observing the other boarders, especially Professor Bhaer, a poor German scholar who supports his orphaned nephews and shows kindness to the children and servants around him. Jo also meets Miss Norton, who invites her into a wider social circle, while Jo grows increasingly interested in Professor Bhaer's character through their small encounters in the house.
moments: 'It goes better so. The little back is too young to haf such heaviness.'

'Thou shalt haf thy Bhaer; come, then, and take a goot hug from him, my Tina,' said the Professor, catching her up, with a laugh, and holding her so high over his head that she had to stoop her little face to kiss him.
'What the deuce is she at our table for?'

chapters.title: XXXIV. A Friend.
chapters.summary: Jo begins writing sensational stories for the Weekly Volcano to earn money for her family and hides the work from her parents. Mr. Dashwood accepts her stories after cutting out the moral passages, and Jo becomes successful enough to build savings for Beth while immersing herself in lurid material that starts to affect her character and imagination. At the same time, she grows increasingly interested in Professor Bhaer, studying his kindness, humility, and intellect until she recognizes him as the kind of man she admires.
moments: "People want to be amused, not preached at, you know. Morals don't sell nowadays;"
"Wrong-doing always brings its own punishment; and, when Jo most needed hers, she got it."

"That's it!" said Jo to herself, when she at length discovered that genuine good-will towards one's fellow-men could beautify and dignify even a stout German teacher, who shovelled in his dinner, darned his own socks, and was burdened with the name of Bhaer.

chapters.title: XXXV. Heartache.
chapters.summary: Laurie graduates with honors and asks Jo to meet him on his return home. During their walk through the grove, he confesses that he has loved her for years and asks her to marry him. Jo refuses him as gently as she can, saying she cares for him deeply as a friend but cannot return his feelings or imagine a happy marriage between them. Laurie leaves in anger and despair, and Jo later tells Mr. Laurence what happened. The rejection changes the relationship between Jo and Laurie and breaks the hopes both families had for their future together.
moments: "I've loved you ever since I've known you, Jo; couldn't help it, you've been so good to me. I've tried to show it, but you wouldn't let me; now I'm going to make you hear, and give me an answer, for I can't go on so any longer."
"I shall always be fond of you, very fond indeed, as a friend, but I'll never marry you; and the sooner you believe it, the better for both of us,—so now!"
"You'll be sorry some day, Jo."

chapters.title: XXXVI. Beth's Secret.
chapters.summary: Jo returns home and realizes that Beth is much sicker than the family understands. She takes Beth to the seaside to recover, but there Beth finally tells Jo that she knows she is dying and has accepted it, while Jo refuses to give up hope. The sisters speak openly about Beth’s fear of leaving home, Jo’s mistaken belief that Beth loved Laurie, and the need to prepare their parents for Beth’s decline. When they return home, Marmee and Mr. March immediately see the truth for themselves.
moments: "Jo, dear, I'm glad you know it. I've tried to tell you, but I couldn't."
"Yes, I gave up hoping then, but I didn't like to own it."

"Jo, dear, don't hope any more; it won't do any good, I'm sure of that. We won't be miserable, but enjoy being together while we wait. We'll have happy times, for I don't suffer much, and I think the tide will go out easily, if you help me."

chapters.title: XXXVII. New Impressions.
chapters.summary: Laurie arrives in Nice on Christmas Day and meets Amy on the Promenade des Anglais. They spend the afternoon driving and talking, and Amy notices that the cheerful boy she knew has become a quieter and more distant man. That evening Amy carefully dresses for a Christmas party because she wants Laurie to admire her, and their reunion begins to shift their relationship from childhood familiarity toward adult attraction.
moments: "O Laurie, is it really you? I thought you'd never come!" cried Amy, dropping the reins, and holding out both hands, to the great scandalization of a French mamma, who hastened her daughter's steps, lest she should be demoralized by beholding the free manners of these "mad English."
"If that's the way he's going to grow up, I wish he'd stay a boy," she thought, with a curious sense of disappointment and discomfort, trying meantime to seem quite easy and gay.

"I do want him to think I look well, and tell them so at home," said Amy to herself, as she put on Flo's old white silk ball-dress, and covered it with a cloud of fresh illusion, out of which her white shoulders and golden head emerged with a most artistic effect.

chapters.title: XXXVIII. On the Shelf.
chapters.summary: Meg becomes consumed by caring for her babies and gradually neglects John, who begins spending his evenings with the Scotts because home feels like a nursery where he no longer has a place. Feeling lonely and resentful, Meg confides in Marmee, who tells her that marriage and parenthood require husband and wife to share both the children and each other’s interests. Meg accepts the advice and resolves to rebuild her home life with John by including him more in family life and restoring companionship between them.
moments: "You have only made the mistake that most young wives make,—forgotten your duty to your husband in your love for your children."
"Don't neglect husband for children, don't shut him out of the nursery, but teach him how to help in it."

"This is just the time, Meg, when young married people are apt to grow apart, and the very time when they ought to be most together; for the first tenderness soon wears off, unless care is taken to preserve it; and no time is so beautiful and precious to parents as the first years of the little lives given them to train."

chapters.title: XXXIX. Lazy Laurence.
chapters.summary: Laurie stays in Nice with Amy longer than planned, and their time together changes how they see each other. Amy grows disappointed with Laurie's idleness and bitterness after Jo rejected him, while Laurie notices Amy's ambition and her practical interest in marrying Fred Vaughn. During a visit to Valrosa, Amy presses Laurie about his future and criticizes his laziness, and their conversation exposes both his aimlessness and her determination to secure wealth and social position.
moments: "Try lower down, and pick those that have no thorns," said Amy, gathering three of the tiny cream-colored ones that starred the wall behind her.
"I want to be great, or nothing. I won't be a common-place dauber, so I don't intend to try any more."
"True, nevertheless."

chapters.title: XL. The Valley of the Shadow.
chapters.summary: Beth’s illness worsens as the March family devotes itself to making her final months peaceful and comfortable. Jo stays constantly at Beth’s side, learns from her patience and faith, and shares a poem that comforts Beth by showing her that her quiet life mattered deeply to those around her. Before dying peacefully in the spring, Beth asks Jo to care for their parents and value love over ambition, a promise that changes Jo’s sense of purpose.
moments: "Then I don't feel as if I'd wasted my life. I'm not so good as you make me, but I have tried to do right; and now, when it's too late to begin even to do better, it's such a comfort to know that some one loves me so much, and feels as if I'd helped them."

"You must take my place, Jo, and be everything to father and mother when I'm gone. They will turn to you, don't fail them; and if it's hard to work alone, remember that I don't forget you, and that you'll be happier in doing that than writing splendid books or seeing all the world; for love is the only thing that we can carry with us when we go, and it makes the end so easy."

"As Beth had hoped, the "tide went out easily;" and in the dark hour before the dawn, on the bosom where she had drawn her first breath, she quietly drew her last, with no farewell but one loving look, one little sigh."

chapters.title: XLI. Learning to Forget.
chapters.summary: Laurie tries to recover from Jo's refusal by devoting himself to music in Vienna, first attempting a Requiem and then an opera. He gradually admits that he lacks the genius to become a great composer, destroys his work, and begins to let go of his romantic attachment to Jo. After Jo rejects him again in a final letter, Laurie puts away her letters and the ring connected to her, then begins a steady correspondence with Amy, while Amy herself refuses Fred Vaughn's proposal and grows increasingly attached to Laurie through their letters.
moments: "She is right! Talent isn't genius, and you can't make it so. That music has taken the vanity out of me as Rome took it out of her, and I won't be a humbug any longer. Now what shall I do?"
"No, I won't! I haven't forgotten, I never can. I'll try again, and if that fails, why, then—"

With a half-repentant, half-amused expression, Laurie gathered up all Jo's letters, smoothed, folded, and put them neatly into a small drawer of the desk, stood a minute turning the ring thoughtfully on his finger, then slowly drew it off, laid it with the letters, locked the drawer, and went out to hear High Mass at Saint Stefan's, feeling as if there had been a funeral; and, though not overwhelmed with affliction, this seemed a more proper way to spend the rest of the day than in writing letters to charming young ladies.

chapters.title: XLII. All Alone.
chapters.summary: Jo struggles after Beth's death. She feels trapped by duty at home, resents the losses in her life, and fears she cannot endure a future built around sacrifice and routine. Her mother, father, and sisters help her through her grief, and Jo begins to change through work, family life, and writing. A story she writes from the heart brings her literary success, and she accepts Amy and Laurie's engagement while admitting her own loneliness and desire for love.
moments: "I can't do it. I wasn't meant for a life like this, and I know I shall break away and do something desperate if somebody don't come and help me," she said to herself, when her first efforts failed, and she fell into the moody, miserable state of mind which often comes when strong wills have to yield to the inevitable.
"Father, talk to me as you did to Beth. I need it more than she did, for I'm all wrong."

"There is truth in it, Jo, that's the secret; humor and pathos make it alive, and you have found your style at last. You wrote with no thought of fame or money, and put your heart into it, my daughter; you have had the bitter, now comes the sweet. Do your best, and grow as happy as we are in your success."

chapters.title: XLIII. Surprises
chapters.summary: Jo spends the evening before her twenty-fifth birthday thinking about growing older, her writing career, and the possibility that she will remain unmarried. Laurie suddenly arrives and tells her that he and Amy married in Paris six weeks earlier after deciding they did not want to separate during their travels. He explains that his romantic feelings for Jo have changed into affection and friendship, and the two agree to leave the past behind and remain brother and sister figures in each other's lives.
moments: "You've gone and got married!"
"I never shall stop loving you; but the love is altered, and I have learned to see that it is better as it is."
"We can't be little playmates any longer, but we will be brother and sister, to love and help one another all our lives, won't we, Laurie?"

chapters.title: XLIV. My Lord and Lady.
chapters.summary: Laurie and Amy settle into married life and talk with the March family about their future. Laurie plans to go into business and work seriously, while Amy imagines building a lively household and social circle. Later, alone together, they discuss Jo and Professor Bhaer, reassure each other about love and money, and decide to use their wealth to quietly help struggling artists, poor gentlepeople, and ambitious young women.
moments: "That man intends to marry our Jo!"
"I'd have married you if you hadn't a penny, and I sometimes wish you were poor that I might show how much I love you;"
"It's a bargain, and we shall get the best of it!"

chapters.title: XLV. Daisy and Demi.
chapters.summary: Meg and John's twins, Daisy and Demi, become the center of the March family as their personalities begin to show. Daisy charms everyone with her affectionate nature, while Demi's curiosity and strange questions lead to long conversations with Mr. March about the mind, God, and how children think. The children also spend much of their time with Jo, and their interactions with Professor Bhaer expose his growing attachment to her, until Demi's innocent questions make Mr. March realize what is happening between them.
moments: "Me loves evvybody," she once said, opening her arms, with her spoon in one hand, and her mug in the other, as if eager to embrace and nourish the whole world.
"I dess Dod does it when I's asleep."
"Do great boys like great girls, too, 'Fessor?"

chapters.title: XLVI. Under the Umbrella.
chapters.summary: Jo and Professor Bhaer fall into a routine of evening walks and visits while Laurie and Amy settle into married life. After Bhaer disappears for several days, Jo goes into the city hoping to see him and meets him by chance in the rain. During their walk and shopping trip together, Bhaer tells her he has accepted a teaching position in the West and plans to leave, while Jo struggles to hide how much the news hurts her.
moments: "It serves me right! What business had I to put on all my best things and come philandering down here, hoping to see the Professor? Jo, I'm ashamed of you! No, you shall not go there to borrow an umbrella, or find out where he is, from his friends. You shall trudge away, and do your errands in the rain; and if you catch your death and ruin your bonnet, it's no more than you deserve. Now then!"
"I haf no longer any business here; it is done."
"Ah! but we shall not meet often, I fear; this place is at the West."

chapters.title: XLVII. Harvest Time.
chapters.summary: Aunt March dies and leaves Plumfield to Jo. Jo decides to turn the estate into a school for boys with Professor Bhaer, and the family rallies around the plan. Over the next several years Plumfield fills with children from different backgrounds, Jo and Fritz build a busy household and school together, and the extended March family gathers there for yearly celebrations that show how their lives have settled into adulthood and family life.
moments: "Boys. I want to open a school for little lads,—a good, happy, homelike school, with me to take care of them, and Fritz to teach them."

"It never was a fashionable school, and the Professor did not lay up a fortune; but it was just what Jo intended it to be,—\"a happy, homelike place for boys, who needed teaching, care, and kindness.\""
"Yes; Jo was a very happy woman there, in spite of hard work, much anxiety, and a perpetual racket."

pride_prejudice.summary: Mrs. Bennet learns that the wealthy Mr. Bingley has rented nearby Netherfield Park and immediately treats him as a possible husband for one of her five daughters. Bingley becomes attached to the eldest daughter, Jane Bennet, while his friend Mr. Darcy offends Elizabeth Bennet with his pride and reserve, and Elizabeth’s dislike deepens after the charming officer Wickham tells her that Darcy cheated him out of an inheritance. Around these courtships, the novel tracks the social and financial pressures on the Bennet family through events including Mr. Collins’s absurd proposal to Elizabeth, Charlotte Lucas’s practical marriage to Collins, and Darcy’s first proposal to Elizabeth at Rosings, which she angrily refuses after accusing him of separating Bingley and Jane and mistreating Wickham. Darcy’s explanatory letter forces Elizabeth to reconsider her judgments, and later visits to Pemberley and Lambton gradually change her feelings as she sees Darcy’s conduct toward his tenants, his sister, and the Gardiners. The crisis of the book comes when Lydia Bennet runs away with Wickham, threatening the reputation and marriage prospects of the whole family, until Darcy secretly locates the couple, pays Wickham’s debts, and arranges their marriage. In the final chapters Bingley and Jane become engaged, Elizabeth accepts Darcy after both have revised their earlier opinions and behavior, and the book ends with the marriages of Jane and Bingley and Elizabeth and Darcy, alongside short accounts of the later lives of the rest of the Bennet family.

chapters.title: Chapter I.
chapters.summary: Mrs. Bennet tells her husband that Netherfield Park has been rented by Mr. Bingley, a wealthy single man from the north of England. She presses Mr. Bennet to visit Bingley so their daughters will have a chance to marry him, while he answers her with sarcasm and jokes at her expense. The chapter introduces the Bennet marriage, Mrs. Bennet’s fixation on marrying off her daughters, and Mr. Bennet’s preference for Lizzy.
moments: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.”

“Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says that Netherfield is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much delighted with it that he agreed with Mr. Morris immediately; that he is to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week.”
“The business of her life was to get her daughters married: its solace was visiting and news.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER II.
chapters.summary: Mr. Bennet surprises his family by revealing that he has already visited Mr. Bingley after pretending for days that he would not. Mrs. Bennet and the girls react with astonishment and excitement because the visit secures an introduction to the wealthy new neighbor, which Mrs. Bennet immediately connects to her daughters’ marriage prospects. The chapter establishes Mr. Bennet’s habit of teasing his family and begins the Bennets’ social connection with Bingley.
moments: “But as I have actually paid the visit, we cannot escape the acquaintance now.”
“How good it was in you, my dear Mr. Bennet! But I knew I should persuade you at last.
“Oh,” said Lydia, stoutly, “I am not afraid; for though I am the youngest, I’m the tallest.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER III.
chapters.summary: Mrs. Bennet and her daughters gather reports about Mr. Bingley after his arrival at Netherfield and build hopes that he may marry one of the Bennet girls. At the local assembly, Bingley wins everyone over with his friendliness and dances twice with Jane Bennet, while his friend Mr. Darcy offends the room with his pride and publicly dismisses Elizabeth as "not handsome enough" to dance with. Elizabeth turns the insult into a joke among her friends, but Mrs. Bennet returns home furious at Darcy and even more determined about Bingley.
moments: “She is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.
Mr. Bingley had danced with her twice, and she had been distinguished by his sisters.
“But I can assure you,” she added, “that Lizzy does not lose much by not suiting his fancy; for he is a most disagreeable, horrid man, not at all worth pleasing.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER IV.
chapters.summary: Jane tells Elizabeth how much she admires Mr. Bingley after the assembly, while Elizabeth jokes about Jane’s habit of thinking well of everyone and admits she distrusts Bingley’s sisters. The chapter explains the Bingley family’s money, social ambitions, and connection to Darcy, whose reserved and proud manner contrasts with Bingley’s easy charm. Bingley leaves the assembly delighted with Jane and the company at Meryton, while Darcy dismisses most of the gathering and finds fault even with Jane’s beauty.
moments: “He is just what a young-man ought to be,” said she, “sensible, good-humoured, lively; and I never saw such happy manners! so much ease, with such perfect good breeding!”
Bingley was sure of being liked wherever he appeared; Darcy was continually giving offence.
Miss Bennet he acknowledged to be pretty; but she smiled too much.

chapters.title: CHAPTER V.
chapters.summary: The Lucases visit Longbourn the morning after the Meryton assembly, and the families discuss Mr. Bingley’s attention to Jane Bennet and Mr. Darcy’s slight toward Elizabeth. Charlotte Lucas repeats Bingley’s praise of Jane, while Mrs. Bennet and Elizabeth mock Darcy’s pride and poor manners. Mary Bennet offers a distinction between pride and vanity, which introduces one of the central conflicts between Elizabeth and Darcy.
moments: ‘Oh, the eldest Miss Bennet, beyond a doubt: there cannot be two opinions on that point.’
“I believe, ma’am, I may safely promise you never to dance with him.”
“That is very true,” replied Elizabeth, “and I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER VI.
chapters.summary: Jane Bennet and Mr. Bingley continue to grow attached, while Elizabeth and Charlotte Lucas argue about whether affection should be openly encouraged in courtship and whether happiness in marriage depends on careful knowledge of a partner. At a gathering at Lucas Lodge, Mr. Darcy becomes increasingly interested in Elizabeth, listens to her conversations, asks her to dance, and later admits to Miss Bingley that he has been thinking about "the very great pleasure which a pair of fine eyes in the face of a pretty woman can bestow." The chapter deepens the contrast between Jane’s reserve, Charlotte’s practical view of marriage, and Elizabeth’s independence, while establishing Darcy’s attraction to Elizabeth.
moments: “In nine cases out of ten, a woman had better show more affection than she feels. Bingley likes your sister undoubtedly; but he may never do more than like her, if she does not help him on.”
“Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.”
“Miss Elizabeth Bennet.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER VII.
chapters.summary: The chapter describes the Bennet family’s financial situation and the younger daughters’ obsession with the militia officers newly stationed in Meryton. Mrs. Bennet schemes to keep Jane at Netherfield by sending her on horseback in bad weather to dine with Miss Bingley, and Jane falls ill after being caught in the rain. Elizabeth walks three miles through mud to care for her sister, impressing Mr. Bingley and attracting Mr. Darcy’s attention while exposing the difference between her practical devotion and the manners valued by the Bingley sisters.
moments: “From all that I can collect by your manner of talking, you must be two of the silliest girls in the country. I have suspected it some time, but I am now convinced.”
“This was a lucky idea of mine, indeed!” said Mrs. Bennet, more than once, as if the credit of making it rain were all her own.
“I shall be very fit to see Jane—which is all I want.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER VIII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth stays at Netherfield while Jane remains ill, and she sees the difference between Bingley’s genuine concern and the indifference of his sisters and Mr. Darcy’s social pride. After dinner, Miss Bingley and Mrs. Hurst mock Elizabeth’s muddy walk to the house and the Bennets’ family connections, while Bingley defends her and Darcy admits her appearance pleased him. Later, the group argues about what makes an accomplished woman, Elizabeth challenges Darcy’s standards, and Jane’s worsening condition leads Bingley to call for the local doctor.
moments: “It shows an affection for her sister that is very pleasing,” said Bingley.
“Not at all,” he replied: “they were brightened by the exercise.”
“All this she must possess,” added Darcy; “and to all she must yet add something more substantial in the improvement of her mind by extensive reading.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER IX.
chapters.summary: Mrs. Bennet visits Jane at Netherfield with Kitty and Lydia and decides Jane should stay there longer because her illness keeps her near Mr. Bingley. Over breakfast, Mrs. Bennet embarrasses Elizabeth with loud praise of Jane’s beauty, insults toward Charlotte Lucas, and awkward conversation with Darcy, while Elizabeth and Darcy spar over character, society, and poetry. Lydia presses Bingley to honor his promise of a ball at Netherfield, and after the Bennets leave, Darcy refuses to join Miss Bingley in mocking Elizabeth.
moments: “Removed!” cried Bingley. “It must not be thought of. My sister, I am sure, will not hear of her removal.”
“I have been used to consider poetry as the food of love,” said Darcy.

“I am perfectly ready, I assure you, to keep my engagement; and, when your sister is recovered, you shall, if you please, name the very day of the ball. But you would not wish to be dancing while she is ill?”

chapters.title: CHAPTER X.
chapters.summary: Jane Bennet slowly recovers at Netherfield while Elizabeth spends more time with the Bingley party. Elizabeth and Darcy argue about pride, friendship, and firmness of character, and their conversation becomes more playful and personal. Darcy grows more attracted to Elizabeth, Miss Bingley notices it and tries to ridicule the idea of a match between them, but Darcy responds by praising Elizabeth’s eyes and shows increasing concern for her company.
moments: “Nothing is more deceitful,” said Darcy, “than the appearance of humility. It is often only carelessness of opinion, and sometimes an indirect boast.”
“Indeed I do not dare.”
“It would not be easy, indeed, to catch their expression; but their colour and shape, and the eyelashes, so remarkably fine, might be copied.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XI.
chapters.summary: Jane joins the evening gathering at Netherfield after dinner, and Bingley gives her constant attention while his sisters try to draw Darcy into conversation. Miss Bingley fails to interest Darcy with reading, talk of a ball, and walking about the room, and Elizabeth instead falls into a lively exchange with Darcy about ridicule, pride, and character. The conversation sharpens the attraction and tension between Elizabeth and Darcy, and Darcy realizes he is becoming too attentive to her.
moments: “You either choose this method of passing the evening because you are in each other’s confidence, and have secret affairs to discuss, or because you are conscious that your figures appear to the greatest advantage in walking: if the first, I should be completely in your way; and if the second, I can admire you much better as I sit by the fire.”

“No,” said Darcy, “I have made no such pretension. I have faults enough, but they are not, I hope, of understanding. My temper I dare not vouch for. It is, I believe, too little yielding; certainly too little for the convenience of the world. I cannot forget the follies and vices of others so soon as I ought, nor their offences against myself. My feelings are not puffed about with every attempt to move them. My temper would perhaps be called resentful. My good opinion once lost is lost for ever.”
He began to feel the danger of paying Elizabeth too much attention.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth asks her mother to send the carriage so she and Jane can leave Netherfield, but Mrs. Bennet tries to keep them there longer in hopes of strengthening Jane’s connection with Mr. Bingley. Mr. Bingley regrets their departure, while Darcy decides to hide his growing attraction to Elizabeth and barely speaks to her before they leave. Back at Longbourn, Mrs. Bennet complains about their return, Mr. Bennet quietly welcomes them, and the younger sisters fill the house with gossip about the militia.
moments: Against staying longer, however, Elizabeth was positively resolved—nor did she much expect it would be asked; and fearful, on the contrary, of being considered as intruding themselves needlessly long, she urged Jane to borrow Mr. Bingley’s carriage immediately, and at length it was settled that their original design of leaving Netherfield that morning should be mentioned, and the request made.

He wisely resolved to be particularly careful that no sign of admiration should now escape him—nothing that could elevate her with the hope of influencing his felicity; sensible that, if such an idea had been suggested, his behaviour during the last day must have material weight in confirming or crushing it.
On Sunday, after morning service, the separation, so agreeable to almost all, took place.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XIII
chapters.summary: Mr. Bennet tells his family that their cousin Mr. Collins will visit Longbourn. He reads Collins’s letter aloud, which announces his wish to end the quarrel between the families, praises his patron Lady Catherine de Bourgh, and hints that he hopes to make amends to the Bennet daughters for inheriting the estate entailed away from them. When Collins arrives, he flatters Mrs. Bennet and her daughters, praises the house and dinner with excessive formality, and awkwardly discusses the entail, establishing himself as a pompous and self-important figure whose presence will affect the family.
moments: “It is from my cousin, Mr. Collins, who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house as soon as he pleases.”

“I cannot be otherwise than concerned at being the means of injuring your amiable daughters, and beg leave to apologize for it, as well as to assure you of my readiness to make them every possible amends; but of this hereafter.”
“There is a mixture of servility and self-importance in his letter which promises well. I am impatient to see him.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XIV
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins spends the evening praising Lady Catherine de Bourgh and describing her daughter and estate in inflated detail. Mr. Bennet encourages him to talk and quietly mocks his vanity, while the rest of the family listens with varying degrees of patience. Later, Mr. Collins refuses to read a novel aloud and chooses Fordyce’s Sermons instead, but Lydia interrupts him with gossip about the militia, leading him to stop reading and retreat to a game of backgammon with Mr. Bennet.
moments: “I have more than once observed to Lady Catherine, that her charming daughter seemed born to be a duchess; and that the most elevated rank, instead of giving her consequence, would be adorned by her.”

“Mr. Bennet’s expectations were fully answered. His cousin was as absurd as he had hoped; and he listened to him with the keenest enjoyment, maintaining at the same time the most resolute composure of countenance, and, except in an occasional glance at Elizabeth, requiring no partner in his pleasure.”
“I have often observed how little young ladies are interested by books of a serious stamp, though written solely for their benefit.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XV.
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins arrives at Longbourn with plans to marry one of the Bennet daughters as compensation for inheriting the estate. After Mrs. Bennet hints that Jane may soon be engaged, he quickly shifts his attention to Elizabeth. During a walk to Meryton, the sisters meet Mr. Wickham, whose tense encounter with Mr. Darcy surprises Elizabeth and raises questions about their history. The chapter also establishes Mr. Collins’s vanity and social awkwardness as he ingratiates himself with the Bennets and Mrs. Philips.
moments: Mr. Collins had only to change from Jane to Elizabeth—and it was soon done—done while Mrs. Bennet was stirring the fire.
Both changed colour, one looked white, the other red.
What could be the meaning of it? It was impossible to imagine; it was impossible not to long to know.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XVI.
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins accompanies the Bennet sisters to their aunt Philips’s gathering in Meryton, where Elizabeth spends the evening talking with Mr. Wickham. Wickham tells her that he grew up with Mr. Darcy and claims that Darcy denied him a church living promised by Darcy’s late father. Elizabeth accepts Wickham’s account and leaves the conversation with a much darker opinion of Darcy’s character.
moments: “His behaviour to myself has been scandalous; but I verily believe I could forgive him anything and everything, rather than his disappointing the hopes and disgracing the memory of his father.”

“The church ought to have been my profession—I was brought up for the church; and I should at this time have been in possession of a most valuable living, had it pleased the gentleman we were speaking of just now.”
“This is quite shocking! He deserves to be publicly disgraced.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XVII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth tells Jane what Wickham said about Mr. Darcy. Jane tries to believe both men and explains the conflict as a misunderstanding, while Elizabeth accepts Wickham’s account and looks forward to judging Darcy for herself at the Netherfield ball. Mr. Bingley and his sisters invite the Bennets to the ball, and Elizabeth is dismayed when Mr. Collins claims the first two dances with her, which makes her realize he may intend to marry her. The family spends the rainy days before the ball in growing anticipation, especially the younger sisters, who are cut off from visiting Meryton and the officers.
moments: “I beg your pardon;—one knows exactly what to think.”

“I am so far from objecting to dancing myself, that I shall hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins in the course of the evening; and I take this opportunity of soliciting yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the two first dances especially; a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to the right cause, and not to any disrespect for her.”

It now first struck her, that she was selected from among her sisters as worthy of being the mistress of Hunsford Parsonage, and of assisting to form a quadrille table at Rosings, in the absence of more eligible visitors.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XVIII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth arrives at the Netherfield ball expecting to see Wickham and learns he has gone to town to avoid Darcy. Angry at Darcy and disappointed by Wickham’s absence, she endures two awkward dances with Mr. Collins before unexpectedly accepting Darcy’s request to dance. During their dance they argue indirectly about Wickham and prejudice, and afterward Miss Bingley and Jane both repeat Darcy’s side of the conflict with Wickham, though Elizabeth refuses to change her opinion of him.
moments: “I do not imagine his business would have called him away just now, if he had not wished to avoid a certain gentleman here.”
“Heaven forbid! That would be the greatest misfortune of all! To find a man agreeable whom one is determined to hate! Do not wish me such an evil.”
“Mr. Wickham is blessed with such happy manners as may insure his making friends; whether he may be equally capable of retaining them, is less certain.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XIX.
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins asks Mrs. Bennet for a private audience with Elizabeth and formally proposes marriage. He explains that he wants a wife because Lady Catherine advised him to marry and because marrying one of the Bennet daughters will ease the injustice of inheriting Longbourn. Elizabeth refuses him repeatedly, but Mr. Collins insists that her rejection follows the usual behavior of young women and assumes she will eventually accept, which pushes Elizabeth toward seeking her father's support.
moments: “Accept my thanks for the compliment you are paying me. I am very sensible of the honour of your proposals, but it is impossible for me to do otherwise than decline them.”
“You could not make me happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who would make you so.”
“Do not consider me now as an elegant female intending to plague you, but as a rational creature speaking the truth from her heart.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XX.
chapters.summary: Mrs. Bennet assumes Elizabeth's refusal of Mr. Collins is only modesty and tries to force the match by appealing to Mr. Bennet. Mr. Bennet instead supports Elizabeth, joking that she will lose one parent either way: her mother if she refuses, her father if she accepts. Mrs. Bennet continues to pressure Elizabeth while Mr. Collins retreats from the proposal, convincing himself that Elizabeth's refusal reflects defects in her character rather than any fault in himself.
moments: “Your mother will never see you again if you do not marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you do.”

“But depend upon it, Mr. Collins,” she added, “that Lizzy shall be brought to reason. I will speak to her about it myself directly. She is a very headstrong, foolish girl, and does not know her own interest; but I will make her know it.”

“Far be it from me,” he presently continued, in a voice that marked his displeasure, “to resent the behaviour of your daughter. Resignation to inevitable evils is the duty of us all: the peculiar duty of a young man who has been so fortunate as I have been, in early preferment; and, I trust, I am resigned.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXI.
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins stays at Longbourn after Elizabeth refuses him and shifts his attention to Charlotte Lucas, while Mrs. Bennet continues to resent Elizabeth’s decision. Elizabeth and Jane meet Wickham in Meryton, and he says he avoided the Netherfield ball so he would not have to spend hours with Darcy. Later Jane receives a letter from Caroline Bingley announcing that the Bingleys have left Netherfield for London and hinting that Mr. Bingley may marry Georgiana Darcy. Jane fears Bingley will not return, but Elizabeth argues that Caroline is trying to separate them because the Bennets are not wealthy enough for the match.
moments: “I found,” said he, “as the time drew near, that I had better not meet Mr. Darcy;—that to be in the same room, the same party with him for so many hours together, might be more than I could bear, and that scenes might arise unpleasant to more than myself.”
“The whole party have left Netherfield by this time, and are on their way to town; and without any intention of coming back again.”

“Miss Bingley sees that her brother is in love with you and wants him to marry Miss Darcy. She follows him to town in the hope of keeping him there, and tries to persuade you that he does not care about you.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXII.
chapters.summary: Charlotte Lucas encourages Mr. Collins after his rejection by Elizabeth Bennet, and he secretly proposes to her at Lucas Lodge. Charlotte accepts because marriage offers financial security and social stability, and her family eagerly approves the match because Mr. Collins will inherit Longbourn. Elizabeth is shocked when Charlotte tells her the news, and the engagement exposes the sharp difference between Charlotte’s practical view of marriage and Elizabeth’s belief that affection should matter.
moments: “Engaged to Mr. Collins! my dear Charlotte, impossible!”

“I am not romantic, you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home; and, considering Mr. Collins’s character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as fair as most people can boast on entering the marriage state.”
“Charlotte, the wife of Mr. Collins, was a most humiliating picture!”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXIII.
chapters.summary: Sir William Lucas visits Longbourn to announce Charlotte Lucas's engagement to Mr. Collins. Mrs. Bennet refuses to believe it, blames Elizabeth for losing Mr. Collins, and grows bitter toward Charlotte and the Lucas family because Charlotte will one day inherit Longbourn through marriage. Elizabeth feels estranged from Charlotte after the engagement, while concern over Bingley's continued absence deepens for both her and Jane as rumors spread that he will not return to Netherfield that winter.
moments: “Good Lord! Sir William, how can you tell such a story? Do not you know that Mr. Collins wants to marry Lizzy?”
Elizabeth felt persuaded that no real confidence could ever subsist between them again.

“Indeed, Mr. Bennet,” said she, “it is very hard to think that Charlotte Lucas should ever be mistress of this house, that I should be forced to make way for her, and live to see her take my place in it!”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXIV.
chapters.summary: Miss Bingley writes to Jane that the Bingleys have settled in London for the winter and speaks enthusiastically about her brother’s closeness to Miss Darcy. Jane accepts the loss quietly and tries to think well of everyone involved, while Elizabeth blames Bingley’s weak character and the influence of his sisters and Mr. Darcy. The chapter deepens the contrast between Jane’s generosity and Elizabeth’s sharper judgments, and it strengthens local resentment against Mr. Darcy as Wickham’s account spreads through Hertfordshire.
moments: “He may live in my memory as the most amiable man of my acquaintance but that is all. I have nothing either to hope or fear, and nothing to reproach him with.

“The more I see of the world the more am I dissatisfied with it; and every day confirms my belief of the inconsistency of all human characters, and of the little dependence that can be placed on the appearance of either merit or sense.
“Thoughtlessness, want of attention to other people’s feelings, and want of resolution, will do the business.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXV.
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins leaves Longbourn after securing his engagement to Charlotte Lucas, and the Gardiners arrive for Christmas. Mrs. Bennet complains about Jane losing Bingley and Elizabeth refusing Collins, while Mrs. Gardiner discusses Jane’s disappointment with Elizabeth and invites Jane to London in hopes that distance will help her recover. During the Gardiners’ visit, Mrs. Gardiner notices Elizabeth’s growing attachment to Wickham, hears more of Wickham’s account of Darcy, and begins to worry about the match.
moments: “It had better have happened to you, Lizzy; you would have laughed yourself out of it sooner. But do you think she would be prevailed on to go back with us? Change of scene might be of service—and perhaps a little relief from home may be as useful as anything.”
“She will drop the acquaintance entirely.”
“I never saw a more promising inclination; he was growing quite inattentive to other people, and wholly engrossed by her.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXVI.
chapters.summary: Mrs. Gardiner warns Elizabeth against becoming attached to Wickham because he has no fortune, and Elizabeth promises to act cautiously, though she admits she likes him very much. Charlotte Lucas marries Mr. Collins and leaves for Kent, while Elizabeth’s friendship with her changes as Charlotte settles into married life at Hunsford. Jane’s letters from London confirm that Miss Bingley has withdrawn from her and that Mr. Bingley has made no effort to see her, which convinces Elizabeth that the relationship is over. Wickham soon shifts his attention to Miss King after she inherits money, and Elizabeth concludes that her feelings for him were never very deep.
moments: “All that I can promise you, therefore, is not to be in a hurry. I will not be in a hurry to believe myself his first object. When I am in company with him, I will not be wishing. In short, I will do my best.”
“I did not think Caroline in spirits,” were her words, “but she was very glad to see me, and reproached me for giving her no notice of my coming to London.

“I am now convinced, my dear aunt, that I have never been much in love; for had I really experienced that pure and elevating passion, I should at present detest his very name, and wish him all manner of evil.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXVII.
chapters.summary: January and February pass quietly at Longbourn while Elizabeth prepares to visit Charlotte Collins at Hunsford. She travels to London with Sir William Lucas and Maria, reunites with Jane at the Gardiners’ house, and learns that Jane still suffers from Bingley’s departure though she has given up hope of renewing the connection. Elizabeth and Mrs. Gardiner argue about Wickham’s pursuit of Miss King after her inheritance, and the chapter ends with Elizabeth eagerly accepting an invitation to join the Gardiners on a summer trip to the Lakes.
moments: “Pray, my dear aunt, what is the difference in matrimonial affairs, between the mercenary and the prudent motive? Where does discretion end, and avarice begin?
“Take care, Lizzy; that speech savours strongly of disappointment.”
“My dear, dear aunt,” she rapturously cried, “what delight! what felicity! You give me fresh life and vigour. Adieu to disappointment and spleen. What are men to rocks and mountains?”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXVIII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth arrives at Hunsford with Sir William and Maria Lucas and is warmly received by Charlotte and Mr. Collins. She observes that Collins remains pompous and self-important, while Charlotte manages her marriage with patience and practical composure. The party learns more about Lady Catherine de Bourgh and receives an invitation to dine at Rosings after Elizabeth catches her first sight of Miss de Bourgh and Mrs. Jenkinson outside the parsonage.
moments: “We dine at Rosings twice every week, and are never allowed to walk home. Her Ladyship’s carriage is regularly ordered for us. I should say, one of her Ladyship’s carriages, for she has several.”
“She looks sickly and cross. Yes, she will do for him very well. She will make him a very proper wife.”

Mr. Collins no sooner saw the two girls than he began to congratulate them on their good fortune, which Charlotte explained by letting them know that the whole party was asked to dine at Rosings the next day.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXIX.
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins brings Elizabeth, Sir William, and Maria Lucas to dine at Rosings, where he takes pride in Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his household. Elizabeth observes Lady Catherine’s commanding manner, Miss de Bourgh’s frail health, and the constant deference shown by Mr. Collins and Sir William. During dinner and after, Lady Catherine questions Elizabeth closely about her family and education, and Elizabeth answers with composure and occasional wit, establishing the tone of their relationship and showing her willingness to resist social intimidation.
moments: “She was not rendered formidable by silence: but whatever she said was spoken in so authoritative a tone as marked her self-importance, and brought Mr. Wickham immediately to Elizabeth’s mind; and, from the observation of the day altogether, she believed Lady Catherine to be exactly what he had represented.”

“But really, ma’am, I think it would be very hard upon younger sisters that they should not have their share of society and amusement, because the elder may not have the means or inclination to marry early.”
“Lady Catherine seemed quite astonished at not receiving a direct answer; and Elizabeth suspected herself to be the first creature who had ever dared to trifle with so much dignified impertinence.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXX.
chapters.summary: Sir William Lucas visits Hunsford and leaves satisfied with Charlotte Collins's marriage and household.
