Elizabeth settles into the routine of the parsonage, watches Lady Catherine de Bourgh dominate the parish and the Collinses' lives, and takes refuge in solitary walks while the family repeatedly dines at Rosings. As Easter approaches, Mr. Darcy arrives at Rosings with Colonel Fitzwilliam and visits the parsonage, where Elizabeth tests Darcy by asking about Jane's stay in London and notices his unease at the subject.
moments: “I may thank you, Eliza, for this piece of civility. Mr. Darcy would never have come so soon to wait upon me.”
“My eldest sister has been in town these three months. Have you never happened to see her there?”

She was perfectly sensible that he never had: but she wished to see whether he would betray any consciousness of what had passed between the Bingleys and Jane; and she thought he looked a little confused as he answered that he had never been so fortunate as to meet Miss Bennet.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXI.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth and the Collinses are invited to Rosings after church on Easter. At Lady Catherine’s house, Colonel Fitzwilliam talks closely with Elizabeth while Darcy watches them, and the conversation turns into a playful argument between Darcy and Elizabeth about pride, social ease, and accomplishment. Elizabeth plays the pianoforte while Lady Catherine interrupts with criticism and advice, and Elizabeth observes Darcy’s behavior toward Anne de Bourgh and concludes that he shows no sign of being attached to his cousin.
moments: “There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at the will of others. My courage always rises with every attempt to intimidate me.”

“I certainly have not the talent which some people possess,” said Darcy, “of conversing easily with those I have never seen before. I cannot catch their tone of conversation, or appear interested in their concerns, as I often see done.”

“My fingers,” said Elizabeth, “do not move over this instrument in the masterly manner which I see so many women’s do. They have not the same force or rapidity, and do not produce the same expression. But then I have always supposed it to be my own fault—because I would not take the trouble of practising. It is not that I do not believe my fingers as capable as any other woman’s of superior execution.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXII.
chapters.summary: Mr. Darcy unexpectedly visits Elizabeth alone at the Parsonage, and their strained conversation circles around Netherfield, Charlotte’s marriage, and the distance between Hunsford and Longbourn. Charlotte later suspects Darcy is in love with Elizabeth, though Elizabeth dismisses the idea because of his awkward silence and reserve. As Darcy and Colonel Fitzwilliam begin visiting the Parsonage almost daily, Elizabeth enjoys Fitzwilliam’s company while Charlotte studies Darcy’s behavior and tries to determine whether his growing attention to Elizabeth is serious.
moments: “My dear Eliza, he must be in love with you, or he would never have called on us in this familiar way.”
“You cannot have a right to such very strong local attachment. You cannot have been always at Longbourn.”

She had once or twice suggested to Elizabeth the possibility of his being partial to her, but Elizabeth always laughed at the idea; and Mrs. Collins did not think it right to press the subject, from the danger of raising expectations which might only end in disappointment; for in her opinion it admitted not of a doubt, that all her friend’s dislike would vanish, if she could suppose him to be in her power.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXIII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth repeatedly encounters Mr. Darcy during her walks in the park at Rosings, and his strange questions make her suspect he may be hinting at Colonel Fitzwilliam’s interest in her. During a walk with Colonel Fitzwilliam, he unknowingly tells her that Darcy recently prevented a friend from making an imprudent marriage, and Elizabeth realizes he means Bingley and Jane. Back at the Parsonage, she concludes that Darcy’s pride and interference caused Jane’s unhappiness, and her anger and distress leave her too ill to attend the evening gathering at Rosings.
moments: “I understood that there were some very strong objections against the lady.”

“I do not see what right Mr. Darcy had to decide on the propriety of his friend’s inclination; or why, upon his own judgment alone, he was to determine and direct in what manner that friend was to be happy.
That he had been concerned in the measures taken to separate Mr. Bingley and Jane, she had never doubted; but she had always attributed to Miss Bingley the principal design and arrangement of them.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXIV.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth rereads Jane’s letters and dwells on Mr. Darcy’s admission that he separated Jane and Bingley. Darcy unexpectedly calls at the parsonage and proposes marriage, declaring his love while also speaking openly about Elizabeth’s lower social connections and his struggle against the match. Elizabeth refuses him and accuses him of ruining Jane’s happiness and mistreating Wickham. Darcy admits he separated Bingley from Jane and leaves after Elizabeth says she could never marry him.
moments: “In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.”
“I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.”
“You could not have made me the offer of your hand in any possible way that would have tempted me to accept it.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXV.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth walks near Rosings after Darcy's proposal and unexpectedly meets him at the park gate. He gives her a letter defending himself against her accusations about Jane and Bingley and about Mr. Wickham. In the letter, Darcy admits that he separated Bingley from Jane because he believed Jane indifferent and disapproved of the Bennet family's behavior, then begins a detailed account of Wickham's upbringing, debts, and broken agreement over a church living.
moments: “I have been walking in the grove some time, in the hope of meeting you. Will you do me the honour of reading that letter?”

“There is but one part of my conduct, in the whole affair, on which I do not reflect with satisfaction; it is that I condescended to adopt the measures of art so far as to conceal from him your sister’s being in town.”
“He resigned all claim to assistance in the church, were it possible that he could ever be in a situation to receive it, and accepted in return three thousand pounds.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXVI.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth reads Darcy’s letter and first rejects his account with anger, especially his explanation for separating Bingley from Jane. As she rereads the letter, she compares Darcy’s claims about Wickham with what she knows and begins to see inconsistencies in Wickham’s conduct and evidence supporting Darcy’s version of events. By the end of the chapter, Elizabeth recognizes her own vanity and prejudice, accepts that she misjudged both men, and feels shame over her family’s behavior and its effect on Jane’s relationship with Bingley.
moments: “This must be false! This cannot be! This must be the grossest falsehood!”

“How despicably have I acted!” she cried. “I, who have prided myself on my discernment! I, who have valued myself on my abilities! who have often disdained the generous candour of my sister, and gratified my vanity in useless or blameless distrust.
“Till this moment, I never knew myself.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXVII.
chapters.summary: Darcy and Colonel Fitzwilliam leave Rosings, and Elizabeth spends her final days there under Lady Catherine’s constant attention and advice about her return journey. Alone, Elizabeth repeatedly rereads Darcy’s letter and reconsiders both his character and her own conduct. She regrets her family’s behavior, worries about Jane’s lost chance with Bingley, and sees Wickham more clearly, while still believing she was right to refuse Darcy.
moments: “But my father cannot. He wrote last week to hurry my return.”
Mr. Darcy’s letter she was in a fair way of soon knowing by heart.
His affection was proved to have been sincere, and his conduct cleared of all blame, unless any could attach to the implicitness of his confidence in his friend.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXVIII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth leaves Hunsford with Maria after a final breakfast conversation with Mr. Collins, who praises his marriage, his connection to Lady Catherine, and the comforts of Rosings. Elizabeth parts affectionately from Charlotte, feeling pity for the life her friend has chosen. On the journey back to the Gardiners, Elizabeth thinks about Darcy’s proposal and struggles to decide how much to tell Jane, especially because any mention of Bingley could reopen Jane’s disappointment.
moments: “We seem to have been designed for each other.”
Elizabeth privately added, “And how much I shall have to conceal!”

To know that she had the power of revealing what would so exceedingly astonish Jane, and must, at the same time, so highly gratify whatever of her own vanity she had not yet been able to reason away, was such a temptation to openness as nothing could have conquered, but the state of indecision in which she remained as to the extent of what she should communicate, and her fear, if she once entered on the subject, of being hurried into repeating something of Bingley, which might only grieve her sister further.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XXXIX.
chapters.summary: Jane and Elizabeth return to Longbourn with Kitty and Lydia, who chatter about shopping, officers, and Wickham. Lydia announces that Mary King has left for Liverpool, ending talk of a match with Wickham, and Elizabeth reflects on her own earlier approval of his pursuit of an heiress. Back at home, Lydia presses for more visits to the militia officers while Elizabeth tries to avoid Wickham and is alarmed to hear that Mrs. Bennet is encouraging a plan for the family to spend the summer near the regiment at Brighton.
moments: “There is no danger of Wickham’s marrying Mary King—there’s for you! She is gone down to her uncle at Liverpool; gone to stay. Wickham is safe.”
“And Mary King is safe!” added Elizabeth; “safe from a connection imprudent as to fortune.”
“I am glad you are come back, Lizzy.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XL.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth tells Jane about Mr. Darcy’s proposal and his letter about Wickham. Jane struggles to believe Wickham capable of such conduct, while Elizabeth admits her own prejudice against Darcy and decides not to expose Wickham publicly. Back at Longbourn, Elizabeth sees that Jane still suffers from her attachment to Bingley, while Mrs. Bennet talks carelessly about Jane’s disappointment and the Collinses’ future claim to the estate.
moments: “There is but such a quantity of merit between them; just enough to make one good sort of man; and of late it has been shifting about pretty much.”
“That it ought not to be attempted. Mr. Darcy has not authorized me to make his communication public.”
“Indeed, I could not. I was uncomfortable enough, I was very uncomfortable—I may say unhappy.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLI.
chapters.summary: Lydia Bennet receives an invitation from Mrs. Forster to go to Brighton with the regiment, which fills Lydia and Mrs. Bennet with excitement and alarms Elizabeth. Elizabeth urges her father to stop the trip, warning that Lydia’s reckless behavior will disgrace the family, but Mr. Bennet dismisses her fears and allows Lydia to go. Before the regiment leaves Meryton, Elizabeth speaks with Wickham and quietly signals that her opinion of Darcy has changed, leaving Wickham uneasy and ending their acquaintance on distant terms.
moments: “If you, my dear father, will not take the trouble of checking her exuberant spirits, and of teaching her that her present pursuits are not to be the business of her life, she will soon be beyond the reach of amendment.
“Let her go, then. Colonel Forster is a sensible man, and will keep her out of any real mischief; and she is luckily too poor to be an object of prey to anybody.

“When I said that he improved on acquaintance, I did not mean that either his mind or manners were in a state of improvement; but that, from knowing him better, his disposition was better understood.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth reflects on her parents’ unhappy marriage and sees more clearly how her father’s contempt for his wife has damaged the family and exposed his daughters to ridicule. After the militia leaves Meryton, Lydia writes shallow letters from Brighton while the household slowly settles into calmer routines. Elizabeth’s planned tour of the Lakes is reduced to a trip through Derbyshire with the Gardiners, and when they propose visiting Pemberley, she secretly fears meeting Darcy before learning that he is supposedly away from home.
moments: “But surely,” said she, “I may enter his county with impunity, and rob it of a few petrified spars, without his perceiving me.”
She felt that she had no business at Pemberley, and was obliged to assume a disinclination for seeing it.
To Pemberley, therefore, they were to go.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLIII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth visits Pemberley with the Gardiners after learning that Mr. Darcy is supposed to be away. She admires the grounds and house, then hears Mrs. Reynolds describe Darcy as a generous landlord, kind master, and devoted brother, which forces Elizabeth to reconsider her judgment of him. In the picture gallery she studies Darcy’s portrait with new feeling, and the visit ends with Darcy unexpectedly arriving at Pemberley and meeting her with startled politeness, leaving Elizabeth ashamed and unsettled.
moments: “And of this place,” thought she, “I might have been mistress! With these rooms I might have now been familiarly acquainted! Instead of viewing them as a stranger, I might have rejoiced in them as my own, and welcomed to them as visitors my uncle and aunt.
“I have never had a cross word from him in my life, and I have known him ever since he was four years old.”
Their eyes instantly met, and the cheeks of each were overspread with the deepest blush.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLIV.
chapters.summary: Mr. Darcy and Georgiana visit Elizabeth and the Gardiners at Lambton earlier than expected, and Bingley soon joins them. The Gardiners begin to suspect Darcy is in love with Elizabeth, while Elizabeth watches Darcy’s changed manners and notices signs that Bingley still cares for Jane. After the visit, Elizabeth lies awake reconsidering her feelings for Darcy and admitting her gratitude, esteem, and growing attachment toward him.
moments: “It is above eight months. We have not met since the 26th of November, when we were all dancing together at Netherfield.”
She certainly did not hate him.

She respected, she esteemed, she was grateful to him, she felt a real interest in his welfare; and she only wanted to know how far she wished that welfare to depend upon herself, and how far it would be for the happiness of both that she should employ the power, which her fancy told her she still possessed, of bringing on the renewal of his addresses.

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLV.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth visits Pemberley with the Gardiners and meets Georgiana Darcy, Miss Bingley, and Mrs. Hurst. Georgiana receives her shyly but politely, while Miss Bingley watches Elizabeth closely and tries to embarrass her by mentioning the militia and indirectly recalling Wickham in front of Darcy and Georgiana. After Elizabeth leaves, Miss Bingley attacks her appearance in an effort to provoke Darcy, but he openly contradicts her and says he now considers Elizabeth one of the handsomest women he knows. The visit confirms Darcy’s continued attachment to Elizabeth and shows Georgiana beginning to admire her as well.
moments: “Pray, Miss Eliza, are not the ——shire militia removed from Meryton? They must be a great loss to your family.”

“Yes,” replied Darcy, who could contain himself no longer, “but that was only when I first knew her; for it is many months since I have considered her as one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance.”
He then went away, and Miss Bingley was left to all the satisfaction of having forced him to say what gave no one any pain but herself.

chapters.title: Chapter XLVI.
chapters.summary: Jane’s letters reach Elizabeth at Lambton with news that Lydia has run away with Wickham. A second letter reports that they may not have gone to Scotland to marry, and that Colonel Forster and Mr. Bennet have failed to trace them beyond London. Elizabeth tells Darcy what has happened and blames herself for concealing Wickham’s character from her family. The scandal convinces her that any future with Darcy is now impossible, even as she realizes how deeply she values him.
moments: “My youngest sister has left all her friends—has eloped; has thrown herself into the power of—of Mr. Wickham.
“But now, as the first shock is over, shall I own that I long for your return?
“Had his character been known, this could not have happened. But it is all, all too late now.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLVII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth travels back to Longbourn with the Gardiners after Lydia’s elopement with Wickham. On the journey, Elizabeth admits that she knows Wickham’s true character from Darcy’s account and blames herself for not warning her family or Lydia before the regiment left Meryton. At Longbourn, Jane still hopes Lydia and Wickham will marry, while Mrs. Bennet falls into hysterics and urges Mr. Gardiner to find the couple in London and prevent Mr. Bennet from fighting Wickham.
moments: “We both know that he has been profligate in every sense of the word; that he has neither integrity nor honour; that he is as false and deceitful as he is insinuating.”
“That such a consequence as this should ensue, you may easily believe was far enough from my thoughts.”
“And if they are not married already, make them marry.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLVIII.
chapters.summary: Mr. Gardiner goes to London to help search for Lydia and Wickham, while the Bennet family waits anxiously for news. Reports spread through Meryton about Wickham’s debts, affairs, and gambling, and Mr. Collins sends a cruel letter advising Mr. Bennet to abandon Lydia and warning that the scandal will damage the other daughters’ prospects. Mr. Bennet eventually returns home without Lydia, blaming himself for allowing her to go to Brighton, and promises stricter control over Kitty and the officers who had frequented the family.
moments: “The death of your daughter would have been a blessing in comparison of this.”
“Say nothing of that. Who should suffer but myself? It has been my own doing, and I ought to feel it.”
“No officer is ever to enter my house again, nor even to pass through the village.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER XLIX.
chapters.summary: Mrs. Hill tells Jane and Elizabeth that an express letter has arrived from Mr. Gardiner. Mr. Gardiner writes that he has found Lydia and Wickham, and that Wickham will marry Lydia if Mr. Bennet agrees to financial terms for her support. Mr. Bennet, Jane, and Elizabeth realize that Mr. Gardiner must have paid Wickham’s debts to secure the marriage, while Mrs. Bennet reacts with excitement and immediately turns her attention to the wedding and Lydia’s future as Mrs. Wickham.
moments: “I have seen them both. They are not married, nor can I find there was any intention of being so; but if you are willing to perform the engagements which I have ventured to make on your side, I hope it will not be long before they are.
“Yes, yes, they must marry. There is nothing else to be done.
“My dear, dear Lydia!” she cried: “this is delightful indeed! She will be married! I shall see her again! She will be married at sixteen!”

chapters.title: CHAPTER L.
chapters.summary: Mr. Bennet agrees to the financial arrangements for Lydia’s marriage to Wickham and reflects on his failure to save money for his family. Mrs. Bennet celebrates the match and plans Lydia’s future without shame, while Mr. Bennet refuses to welcome the couple freely into Longbourn or spend money on Lydia’s wedding clothes. Elizabeth regrets telling Mr. Darcy about the elopement and realizes she could have been happy with him, even as she concludes that Lydia’s marriage has ended any possibility between them. Mr. Gardiner later reports that Wickham will leave the militia for a regiment in the north, and the Bennets finally agree to receive the newly married couple at Longbourn before they depart.
moments: “Into one house in this neighbourhood they shall never have admittance. I will not encourage the imprudence of either, by receiving them at Longbourn.”
She was convinced that she could have been happy with him, when it was no longer likely they should meet.
He has the promise of an ensigncy in General——’s regiment, now quartered in the north.

chapters.title: CHAPTER LI.
chapters.summary: Lydia and Wickham arrive at Longbourn after their wedding and behave with complete ease, while Elizabeth and Jane feel ashamed and distressed by their lack of embarrassment. Lydia boasts about her marriage, claims precedence over Jane as a married woman, and talks openly about the elopement. Later, Lydia accidentally reveals that Mr. Darcy attended the wedding, which shocks Elizabeth and leads her to write to Mrs. Gardiner for an explanation of his involvement.
moments: “Ah, Jane, I take your place now, and you must go lower, because I am a married woman.”
“However, I recollected afterwards, that if he had been prevented going, the wedding need not be put off, for Mr. Darcy might have done as well.”
“Mr. Darcy!” repeated Elizabeth, in utter amazement.

chapters.title: CHAPTER LII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth receives a long letter from Mrs. Gardiner explaining that Mr. Darcy found Lydia and Wickham in London, negotiated their marriage, paid Wickham’s debts, and arranged his commission. Mrs. Gardiner also says Darcy insisted on handling the matter himself and hints that his attachment to Elizabeth influenced his actions. Elizabeth realizes the extent of Darcy’s efforts and reconsiders her feelings toward him with gratitude, admiration, and regret for her past judgments, before an awkward conversation with Wickham interrupts her reflections.
moments: “Mr. Darcy called, and was shut up with him several hours.”

“He had followed them purposely to town, he had taken on himself all the trouble and mortification attendant on such a research; in which supplication had been necessary to a woman whom he must abominate and despise, and where he was reduced to meet, frequently meet, reason with, persuade, and finally bribe the man whom he always most wished to avoid, and whose very name it was punishment to him to pronounce.”
“Her heart did whisper that he had done it for her.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LIII.
chapters.summary: Lydia and Wickham leave Longbourn for Newcastle, and Mrs. Bennet quickly turns her attention to the news that Mr. Bingley is returning to Netherfield. Jane tries to appear indifferent to Bingley’s arrival, while Elizabeth wonders whether he still cares for Jane and whether Darcy has come with him by choice. When Bingley and Darcy visit Longbourn, Elizabeth struggles with her changed feelings toward Darcy and with the embarrassment caused by her mother’s behavior toward both men.
moments: “Let me first see how he behaves,” said she; “it will then be early enough for expectation.”
“Could I expect it to be otherwise?” said she. “Yet why did he come?”

But Elizabeth had sources of uneasiness which could not yet be suspected by Jane, to whom she had never yet had courage to show Mrs. Gardiner’s letter, or to relate her own change of sentiment towards him.

chapters.title: CHAPTER LIV.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth tries to understand Darcy’s cold and silent behavior after his visit to Longbourn, while Jane insists she can now meet Bingley without embarrassment. At a dinner party, Bingley openly returns his attention to Jane by sitting beside her and showing clear admiration, which convinces Elizabeth that he still loves her sister. Elizabeth hopes for a private conversation with Darcy, but repeated interruptions and social obligations keep them apart, while Mrs. Bennet grows certain that Bingley will soon propose to Jane.
moments: “If he does not come to me, then,” said she, “I shall give him up for ever.”
On entering the room, he seemed to hesitate; but Jane happened to look round, and happened to smile: it was decided. He placed himself by her.
“I think you are in very great danger of making him as much in love with you as ever.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LV.
chapters.summary: Mr. Bingley resumes his visits to Longbourn, and Mrs. Bennet repeatedly tries to leave him alone with Jane. After several awkward attempts, Bingley proposes to Jane while the family is occupied elsewhere, and Jane happily accepts him. The engagement changes the mood of the household, restores the match that had been interrupted earlier in the novel, and confirms Elizabeth’s belief that Mr. Darcy helped bring Bingley back.
moments: Jane could have no reserves from Elizabeth, where confidence would give pleasure; and, instantly embracing her, acknowledged, with the liveliest emotion, that she was the happiest creature in the world.
“Jane, I congratulate you. You will be a very happy woman.”
“He has made me so happy,” said she, one evening, “by telling me that he was totally ignorant of my being in town last spring! I had not believed it possible.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LVI.
chapters.summary: Lady Catherine de Bourgh arrives unexpectedly at Longbourn after hearing reports that Elizabeth Bennet may marry Mr. Darcy. She takes Elizabeth aside and demands that she deny the rumor and promise never to accept Darcy, arguing that he is intended for her daughter and that Elizabeth’s family connections make the match improper. Elizabeth refuses to give any promise, defends her right to choose for herself, and withstands Lady Catherine’s insults and pressure.
moments: “Tell me, once for all, are you engaged to him?”
“I will make no promise of the kind.”
“I am only resolved to act in that manner, which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LVII.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth turns over Lady Catherine’s visit and fears that Lady Catherine will pressure Darcy to give her up. She decides that if Darcy does not return to Netherfield she will accept that he chose pride and family approval over her. The next morning Mr. Bennet receives a letter from Mr. Collins repeating the rumor that Elizabeth will marry Darcy, and he laughs at the idea while Elizabeth struggles to hide her distress and uncertainty about Darcy’s feelings.
moments: “If, therefore, an excuse for not keeping his promise should come to his friend within a few days,” she added, “I shall know how to understand it. I shall then give over every expectation, every wish of his constancy. If he is satisfied with only regretting me, when he might have obtained my affections and hand, I shall soon cease to regret him at all.”
“My motive for cautioning you is as follows:—We have reason to imagine that his aunt, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, does not look on the match with a friendly eye.”
“Yes, that is what makes it amusing. Had they fixed on any other man it would have been nothing; but his perfect indifference and your pointed dislike make it so delightfully absurd!”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LVIII.
chapters.summary: Darcy returns to Longbourn with Bingley, and during a walk Elizabeth finally thanks him for arranging Lydia’s marriage. Darcy admits he acted for her sake and asks whether her feelings have changed since his first proposal. Elizabeth accepts him, and they speak openly about Lady Catherine’s interference, Darcy’s earlier behavior, his letter, and the changes in both of them since Rosings and Pemberley. On the way home, Darcy explains how he encouraged Bingley to renew his courtship of Jane after admitting his earlier interference had been wrong.
moments: “If you will thank me,” he replied, “let it be for yourself alone. That the wish of giving happiness to you might add force to the other inducements which led me on, I shall not attempt to deny. But your family owe me nothing. Much as I respect them, I believe I thought only of you.”

“You are too generous to trifle with me. If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once. My affections and wishes are unchanged; but one word from you will silence me on this subject for ever.”

“Such I was, from eight to eight-and-twenty; and such I might still have been but for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not owe you! You taught me a lesson, hard indeed at first, but most advantageous. By you, I was properly humbled. I came to you without a doubt of my reception. You showed me how insufficient were all my pretensions to please a woman worthy of being pleased.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LIX.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth returns from her walk with Darcy after accepting his proposal and confides in Jane, who struggles at first to believe the engagement because Elizabeth had once disliked him so strongly. Elizabeth and Darcy arrange to seek her parents’ consent. Mr. Bennet questions whether Elizabeth can truly respect and love Darcy, but she convinces him by explaining her changed opinion and revealing Darcy’s role in Lydia’s marriage. Mrs. Bennet reacts with astonishment and delight once she learns of Darcy’s wealth and status, and the family begins to accept the match.
moments: “He still loves me, and we are engaged.”

“I do, I do like him,” she replied, with tears in her eyes; “I love him. Indeed he has no improper pride. He is perfectly amiable. You do not know what he really is; then pray do not pain me by speaking of him in such terms.”
“Good gracious! Lord bless me! only think! dear me! Mr. Darcy! Who would have thought it? And is it really true?”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LX.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth and Darcy speak openly about how they fell in love and how Lady Catherine’s attempt to separate them pushed Darcy to propose again. Elizabeth writes to the Gardiners with the news of her engagement, and the chapter follows the reactions of their families and acquaintances, including Miss Bingley, Georgiana Darcy, Mr. Bennet, and the Collinses. As Darcy endures the manners of Elizabeth’s relations during the courtship, Elizabeth looks ahead to their future life together at Pemberley.
moments: “I was in the middle before I knew that I had begun.”
“Lady Catherine’s unjustifiable endeavours to separate us were the means of removing all my doubts.”
“I am the happiest creature in the world. Perhaps other people have said so before, but no one with such justice.”

chapters.title: CHAPTER LXI.
chapters.summary: Elizabeth and Darcy settle into married life at Pemberley, while Jane and Bingley move closer to them after leaving Netherfield. The chapter follows the later fortunes of the Bennet family: Kitty improves under her sisters’ influence, Mary remains at home with Mrs. Bennet, and Lydia and Wickham continue their careless and debt-ridden life while depending on help from Elizabeth and Jane. Darcy reconciles with Lady Catherine, Georgiana grows close to Elizabeth, and the novel closes with the enduring ties between the Darcys, the Bingleys, and the Gardiners.
moments: “Mr. Bingley and Jane remained at Netherfield only a twelvemonth.”

“His affection for her soon sunk into indifference: hers lasted a little longer; and, in spite of her youth and her manners, she retained all the claims to reputation which her marriage had given her.”

“But at length, by Elizabeth’s persuasion, he was prevailed on to overlook the offence, and seek a reconciliation; and, after a little further resistance on the part of his aunt, her resentment gave way, either to her affection for him, or her curiosity to see how his wife conducted herself; and she condescended to wait on them at Pemberley, in spite of that pollution which its woods had received, not merely from the presence of such a mistress, but the visits of her uncle and aunt from the city.”
